title: Take Me Home Tonight
full_review:
Those with an irresistible urge to hear Dexys Midnight Runners implore Eileen -- whoever she may have been -- to "Come On" just one more time or who wish to be reminded that the members of Duran Duran were once "Hungry Like the Wolf" can fulfill their unusual yearnings by seeking out the soundtrack of "Take Me Home Tonight" (Relativity).

As for this slack, morally heedless coming-of-age comedy itself, however, like certain aspects of the past, musical and otherwise, it's best forgotten.

Set in 1988 Los Angeles, the film chronicles a transformative night in the life of recent MIT graduate Matt Franklin (Topher Grace). Unable to commit to a serious career path, Matt instead fritters his time away as a clerk in a mall video store.

Through a series of adventures that includes stealing a car, attending a wild party and posing as a high-powered investment banker in order to impress, and hopefully bed, his elusive high school crush Tori (Teresa Palmer), with whom he has recently reconnected, Matt somehow learns a lesson in maturity. Or so, at least, we're asked to believe.

Matt is accompanied, on his merry way, by his mischievous best friend Barry (Dan Fogler) and his sexually unabashed twin sister Wendy (Anna Faris).

Barry experiences some wild times of his own during a casual onscreen encounter with an older woman he's just met, throughout which -- much to Barry's distress -- her voyeuristic boyfriend hovers in close proximity.

More to Barry's liking is a baggie full of nose candy that -- this being the late '80s, after all -- turns up out of the blue.

And so it goes as, seemingly nostalgic for consequence-free hedonism, rather than any form of innocence, co-writer and director Michael Dowse celebrates his youthful ensemble's sowing of some thoroughly distasteful wild oats.

The film contains strong sexual content -- including graphic nonmarital sexual activity, voyeurism and upper female nudity; drug use; about 10 instances of profanity; and pervasive rough and crude language. The Catholic News Service classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
